newsitem.title: UK: Cold light of day casts doubt on UK budget plans.
newsitem.headline: Cold light of day casts doubt on UK budget plans.

text.p: UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke unveiled what he termed a prudent budget on Tuesday but in the cold light of day, economists said there were serious doubts about his inflation target and deficit plans.
The budget forecast that consumer spending will leap by 4.25 percent next year did not square with the government's objective of reducing underlying inflation to 2.5 percent, analysts said.
And a public sector debt target of 19 billion stg next year, helped by tough spending reductions and a crackdown on benefit fraud, took some swallowing, they added.
Clarke's budget cut the basic rate of income tax by a modest one percentage point, to 23 percent and raised spending on the political hot potatoes of health and education.

But compensating spending cuts and tax rises elsewhere added up to a package in which tax giveaways worth about two billion stg were matched by the same amount of spending cuts -- "a sensible, virtuous budget" Clarke said.

But economists said a policy mix of tax cuts, spending cuts and the prospect of higher interest rates was precisely the wrong one for an economy where exporters are struggling while consumer spending is soaring.
"He's given far too much to the consumer sector," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.
Clarke pinned his hopes for enduringly low inflation on the absence of pipeline inflation pressures. Factory gate producer prices are only rising a little over two percent year-on-year.
But if the government is right about high street spending, retailers will face a huge temptation to try and rebuild price margins, squeezed throughout the 1990s.
A leap in underlying retail price inflation, excluding mortgage interest payments, to 3.3 percent year-on-year in October may have been an early sign of that.

"The new measures do little to solve the economy's main problem -- the problem of rising inflation," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers. "Indeed, by including almost three billion stg of reductions in personal taxes, the budget will probably make matters worse."
As a result, most economists said the budget was not tight enough to prevent increases in interest rates.

A Reuter poll of 35 London-based economists showed a consensus expecting base rates, now at 6.00 percent, to be at seven percent by the end of next year. At least a quarter-point rise is likely to come before elections due within six months.
If Clarke's thinking on inflation was wistful, his projections for Britain's famously stubborn public sector debt were little short of fanciful, economists said.

Clarke slashed his public sector borrowing requirement for 1997/98 from 23.1 billion stg to 19 billion, seven billion below this year's PSBR forecast. He also said the government's accounts would be broadly in balance by the turn of the century.
Economists at Goldman Sachs said the Treasury's sums for the PSBR were doubtful, including income from extra asset sales, closing tax loopholes and measures to "secure the tax base."
"In other words, over 4.0 billion stg of tightening measures seem to be semi-conjuring tricks," they said in a budget note.

Clarke pledged to crack down on benefit fraud and get Inland Revenue experts to probe how "big, sophisticated companies pay so little tax." He also said he would put an end to "some of the clever wheezes" dreamed up to avoid paying Value-Added-Tax. This so-called "spend to save package" would cost 800 million stg over three years but recoup 6.7 billion stg, Clarke forecast.
"What really worries me is the rather nebulous figure about how much is to be raised by clamping down on fraud and the black economy," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident.
Andy Cates, UK economist at UBS, said the medium-term public borrowing plans factored in GDP growth of 2.25 percent for each of the next four years, boosting tax revenues.
"The Treasury's assumptions about how quickly the economy will grow over the next four years and along with it how fast revenues will rise are too optimistic," he said.

Andrew Snowball, UK economist at the Cooperative Bank also poured scorn on the spending targets. "The government's spending targets are unlikely to met...and the pressures are likely to get worse not better as the election approaches."
